candidate.answerReason: Subtracting three times the first polynomial from the second gives -14(x²-2x+5). The common monic quadratic must therefore be x²-2x+5, which divides both original polynomials and has value 4 at 1.

methods.label: Eliminate the fourth-degree terms
methods.explanation:
A common factor also divides the difference of polynomial multiples. Here the leading coefficients suggest subtracting three times the first polynomial from the second, which removes the fourth-degree terms.

Write
\[
F(x)=x^4+6x^2+25,\qquad
G(x)=3x^4+4x^2+28x+5.
\]
Since \(p\) divides both, there are polynomials \(U,V\) with \(F=pU\) and \(G=pV\). Therefore \(G-3F=p(V-3U)\), so \(p\) divides
\[
\begin{aligned}
G-3F&=-14x^2+28x-70\\
&=-14(x^2-2x+5).
\end{aligned}
\]
This difference has degree two, just like \(p\), so their quotient is a constant. Since \(p\) has leading coefficient \(1\), that constant must be \(-14\). Hence
\[
p(x)=x^2-2x+5.
\]
The coefficients are integers, and the original divisibilities are confirmed by
\[
\begin{aligned}
F&=(x^2-2x+5)(x^2+2x+5),\\
G&=(x^2-2x+5)(3x^2+6x+1).
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus \(p(1)=1-2+5=4\), choice D.
